audio_segments.text: An AI agent can extend its capabilities by using tools.
A tool might be a small function, such as a calculator, or an API call to an external service.
The model generates a function call that identifies the tool and its arguments.
The function then runs, and its result returns to the model.
Keep those responsibilities clear: selecting a tool, executing its code, and composing the response are
separate steps.
The lesson groups tool use around tasks that need interaction with external systems.
Information retrieval can query an API or database.
Code execution can support calculations, reports or simulations.
Workflow automation connects several operations, while support agents can interact with customer
systems or knowledge bases.
Content tools can check, summarise or evaluate text.
Begin with the task, then identify which tool capability it requires.
A working tool-use design needs more than a function description.
Schemas define what is available.
Execution logic decides how and when a tool is invoked.
Message handling connects user inputs, model responses, calls and results.
Integration connects the actual tools.
Error handling and validation deal with failures, parameters and unexpected responses.
State management preserves context and earlier interactions across turns.
These are six distinct responsibilities, even when a framework provides several of them together.
The source illustrates a time lookup tool.
Its schema gives the name get current time, explains its purpose, and describes a location parameter.
That parameter is a string and is required.
This description helps the model construct a request.
It does not execute the lookup.
Developers still need a model that supports function calling, the function descriptions, and the
implementation of every function they expose.
Follow the complete loop.
Send the user request and the available function descriptions to the model.
The model can return a function name and arguments.
Your application executes the corresponding function.
The result is sent back to the model, which uses it to respond.
In the source example, a call identifier links the function output to its call.
A returned tool call is an intermediate request to run code; it is not yet the answer to the user.
The lesson shows two ways to connect tools.
With Microsoft Agent Framework, decorated Python functions can be serialised into schemas, and the
framework handles the exchange between the model and the code.
Tools may also come from a server using the Model Context Protocol, or MCP.
The framework reads the server’s tool schemas and offers those tools alongside local ones.
When a remote tool is used, the generated query is sent to that server.
The source’s managed-service example groups tools into two categories.
Knowledge tools include search and file retrieval.
Action tools include function calling and code interpretation.
A toolset makes multiple tools available together, while threads keep the history of a conversation.
The service example also handles tool invocation and responses on the server.
Keep the toolset and the thread distinct: one organises capabilities; the other retains messages.
Tools can touch real systems, so their permissions matter.
The lesson highlights risks from model-generated SQL, including injection and database tampering.
It recommends restricting database access to read-only operations and, for the database services
it names, assigning a read-only select role.
It also describes a secure environment and a read-only analytical database or warehouse.
The implementation decision is concrete: the application’s database access should match the
restricted reading task.
Consider this original question based on the source’s time lookup.
A user asks for the current time in a city.
The model returns the function name get current time and the location arguments.
Has the user’s question already been answered?
Name the next two application steps before revealing the solution.
The tool call is not yet the final answer.
First, execute the selected function with the supplied location.
Next, return its result to the model, preserving the call identifier used in the source example.
The model can then use that result to answer the user.
Recall the larger design: describe tools clearly, connect execution and messages, preserve state, and
validate inputs and results.
